power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Antenatal depression is common, under-detected, and harms mothers and infants.
Pakistan has Asia's highest perinatal depression prevalence and an estimated national economic burden of US$16.5 billion.
About 9.7 million Pakistani women become pregnant each year, and roughly 3.6 million may experience antenatal depression.
Routine detection relies on self-report scales (e.g., Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale [EPDS]); whether biomarkers add prognostic value is largely untested.
Objective: Develop and validate a multivariable prognostic tool (MPT) to predict clinically significant depressive symptoms (EPDS ≥ 10) and assess the added value of biomarker data.
Methods: We will use secondary data (N = 1,621) from the Pakistani Pregnancy Cohort at the Aga Khan Hospital for Women and Children, Sindh.

Self-reported predictors across eight domains (demographic, socioeconomic, behavioural, mental health, clinical history, pregnancy-related, and social network) plus biomarkers will inform MPT development.
In Stage 1 we will compare supervised classifiers (regularized regression, decision trees, support vector machines, and neural networks) to logistic regression.

Models will be trained with stratified five-fold cross-validation and nested L1 selection within folds to retain the smallest predictor set within 0.01 area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of the full mode.

External cross-validation on an independent hold-out sample will report ROC-AUC, area under the precision-recall curve (relative to prevalence), calibration, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values.
Decision thresholds will be set on training data and applied unchanged.

In Stage 2 we will build a biomarker-augmented model and compare it to the optimized self-report model using paired AUC tests and reclassification metrics; exploratory clustering will identify participant subgroups.
Pre-specified criteria (ROC-AUC ≥ 0.70; calibration slope 0.8-1.2; sensitivity ≥ 0.70; positive net benefit) will determine progression to prospective validation studies in new samples.
Expected Outcomes: A pragmatic self-report prognostic tool and evidence on whether biomarkers meaningfully improve prediction and justify added complexity.

text.text: We present the protocol and statistical plan for developing a two-stage MPT that uses earlypregnancy data (10-19 weeks' gestation) to correctly classify cases with clinically significant depressive symptoms in the late second trimester.
In stage 1 we will derive an initial classifier model using self-reported measures for all participants.

In stage 2 we will identify the subgroup for whom the self-report model shows limited discrimination and evaluate whether adding biomarker data improves classification accuracy compared with the self-report model alone.

We used an integrated knowledge-translation approach and co-designed the study with researchers, clinicians, laboratory staff, and policymakers during two planning meetings, including a 2012 CIHR-funded meeting.

text.text: Prior to model development, all features will undergo data cleaning.

We will audit raw data for structural errors (duplicate records, inconsistent coding, and implausible values such as biologically impossible biomarker results or out-of-range gestational age entries) and correct or flag issues in consultation with the clinical research team.

Continuous features will be inspected visually (e.g., histograms, boxplots) and with standard statistical criteria (e.g., interquartile range) to characterize distributions and identify outliers; each outlier will be reviewed individually to distinguish data-entry errors from valid extreme observations.
Categorical variables will be checked for consistent labelling and, where necessary, collapsed to avoid sparse categories that could affect model estimates.
We will encode categorical features according to their type and modeling needs: ordinal features such as maternal education will receive integer mappings, nominal features will be one-hot encoded.
All encoders will be fitted on the training partition (or within each cross-validation fold) and applied unchanged to validation/test data to avoid information leakage [49, 50].

text.text: We selected a GMM over traditional latent class analysis for three reasons.
First, our predictor set contains both continuous and categorical (one-hot encoded) variables, and GMMs can accommodate mixed feature types without discretization or exclusion.
Second, GMMs provide posterior probabilities for class membership, preserving assignment uncertainty for downstream analyses rather than yielding only hard clusters.
Third, class number can be chosen in a data-driven way using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), GMMs allow classspecific covariance structures.
Because treating binary indicators as Gaussian is an approximation, resulting class solutions will be treated as exploratory.
Model will be fitted on the training partition only, testing two to seven classes with five random starts per solution and a fixed seed for reproducibility.

We will select the optimal solution according to pre-specified criteria: minimum BIC; mean silhouette coefficient > 0.25 (acceptable cluster structure) [77]; entropy ≥ 0.8 (adequate class separation) [78]; minimum class size of ≥ 5% to ensure stable parameter estimates [79]; and clinical interpretability of the profiles.

text.text: The ROC-AUC will be the primary discriminative metric [84, 85]; secondary metrics will include calibration, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value.

text.text: We will compared observed performance with benchmarks in mental-health prediction studies which have reported ROC-AUC values ranging from 0.59 to 0.71 [86].

text.text: As a reference benchmark, we consider a ROC-AUC of 0.70 with balanced sensitivity and specificity above 70%, but all results will be reported and interpreted transparently regardless of whether these thresholds are met [87].

text.text: After cross-validation, we will retain the best-performing classifier on the full training sample using the optimal hyperparameters and generate individual predicted probabilities for the independent hold-out test set.
Final performance on the test set will be reported using ROC-AUC and the specified secondary metrics, and results will be presented in accordance with TRIPOD+AI reporting guidance [88].
text.formatted: Final performance on the test set will be reported using ROC-AUC and the specified secondary metrics, and results will be presented in accordance with TRIPOD+AI reporting guidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">[88]</ref>.

text.text: We will empirically evaluate whether biomarkers add predictive value beyond self-reported measures rather than assume they do [46].
text.formatted: We will empirically evaluate whether biomarkers add predictive value beyond self-reported measures rather than assume they do <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref>.

text.text: First, we will optimize the selected self-report classifier using the training data and internal cross-validation.
Next, we will develop a biomarker-augmented version of that classifier by adding available biomarker variables to the same predictor set.
Both models will be compared within the same validation framework to assess whether the biomarker-augmented model improves discrimination.
We will use paired tests of correlated ROC-AUCs [89] and reclassification-based measures to quantify incremental predictive value [90].
text.formatted: We will use paired tests of correlated ROC-AUCs <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">[89]</ref> and reclassification-based measures to quantify incremental predictive value <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">[90]</ref>.

text.text: The top performing classifier will then be retrained on the full training sample with the optimal hyperparameters and used to generate individual predicted probabilities in the held-out test set.
We will assess performance on the independent test set using ROC-AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and calibration metrics [88].
text.formatted: We will assess performance on the independent test set using ROC-AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and calibration metrics <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">[88]</ref>.

text.text: If biomarkers yield a meaningful improvement in out-of-sample performance, the biomarker-augmented model will be considered for further clinical implementation; if not, we will retain the self-report model as the primary, pragmatic option.
Consistent with our co-design approach, we will present the Stage 1 (self-report) and Stage 2 (biomarker-augmented) classifiers to the CAB before any hold-out testing.
The materials will include the chosen predictors, the empirically derived classification threshold, and the indeterminate-range criterion that defines eligibility for biomarker testing.
The CAB will assess clinical relevance, cultural appropriateness, and feasibility for routine care and may recommend adjustments to thresholds, predictors, or feasible biomarker collection.
Any changes that require model refitting will be implemented using the training partition only.

We will complete this iterative CAB review and any consequent retraining prior to evaluating final performance on the independent hold-out test set, ensuring the hold-out data remain untouched throughout model development and threshold setting.
We will apply the trained classifiers sequentially to the independent hold-out sample.
First, the Stage 1 self-report classifier will produce a predicted probability for each hold-out participant.

Participants with probabilities falling in the prespecified indeterminate range will also be evaluated with the Stage 2 biomarker-augmented classifier using their biomarker values; participants outside the indeterminate range will retain their Stage 1 classification.
The combined predictions across the full hold-out sample will constitute the final outputs of the two-stage strategy.
Discrimination will be quantified using ROC-AUC.

Classification performance will be summarized with a confusion matrix reporting accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, and calibration will be examined with plots comparing observed versus predicted event probabilities.

Clinical utility will be evaluated with decision-curve analysis [91] to estimate net benefit across probability thresholds and to compare the selective two-stage strategy with a universal biomarker-testing approach and with treat-all and treat-none benchmarks.
text.formatted: Clinical utility will be evaluated with decision-curve analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">[91]</ref> to estimate net benefit across probability thresholds and to compare the selective two-stage strategy with a universal biomarker-testing approach and with treat-all and treat-none benchmarks.

text.text: Finally, we will report the proportion of participants requiring biomarker testing under the two-stage strategy as a pragmatic measure of implementation efficiency.
The analytic sample comprises 1,621 participants with complete outcome data at 22-29 weeks' gestation and 1594 participants with complete biomarker data.
Recommended practice is to target roughly 10-20 outcome events per candidate predictor to reduce overfitting and produce stable estimates [92].
text.formatted: Recommended practice is to target roughly 10-20 outcome events per candidate predictor to reduce overfitting and produce stable estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">[92]</ref>.

text.text: The analytic sample will be split into training (n = 1,135) and an independent hold-out sample (n = 486).

Required sample-sizes for prediction models depend on context, but simulation and learning-curve studies generally indicate that several hundred cases are needed for stable, generalizable performance.

Guidance recommends at least 300 patients per arm for multivariate treatment-selection models in depression, and empirical studies indicate predictive performance typically stabilizes at roughly n = 300 for psychotherapy-dropout outcomes [93, 94].
text.formatted: Guidance recommends at least 300 patients per arm for multivariate treatment-selection models in depression, and empirical studies indicate predictive performance typically stabilizes at roughly n = 300 for psychotherapy-dropout outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">[93,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">94]</ref>.

text.text: Both our training and hold-out samples exceed these pragmatic benchmarks.
With up to 42 candidate predictors, the available sample size is expected to be adequate provided with a plausible prevalence of EDPS ≥ 10.
We will verify this once the outcome prevalence in the analytic sample is known.

If events per variable are insufficient for a given model, we will reduce dimensionality before fitting: preferred strategies include penalized (regularized) regression, cross-validated variable selection or dimensionality reduction (e.g., principal component or factor scores), and, if required, an a priori, theorydriven predictor subset informed by the CAB.
Regularization and cross-validation will be prioritized because they preserve predictive information while mitigating overfitting.
Clinically significant depressive symptoms (EPDS ≥ 10) are expected to be a minority outcome in this antenatal sample [95, 96].
text.formatted: Clinically significant depressive symptoms (EPDS ≥ 10) are expected to be a minority outcome in this antenatal sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">[95,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">96]</ref>.

text.text: Because overall accuracy can be misleading under such class imbalance [97]; we will prioritize performance metrics that are robust to class imbalance, principally precision-recall (pr) AUC and calibration [98].
text.formatted: Because overall accuracy can be misleading under such class imbalance <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">[97]</ref>; we will prioritize performance metrics that are robust to class imbalance, principally precision-recall (pr) AUC and calibration <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">[98]</ref>.

text.text: If imbalance materially impairs classifier training, we will apply mitigation strategies (for example, class-weighted loss functions or minority oversampling) exclusively within the training partition [81], leaving the hold-out test set unchanged to preserve its real-world outcome distribution.

text.text: Because rebalancing can preserve discrimination while degrading probability calibration [99], we will adopt mitigation only when it improves cross-validated discrimination and will explicitly evaluate its impact on calibration before use.

text.text: Consistent with the study's equity aims, we will evaluate model performance across prespecified subgroups including socioeconomic status, recruitment site, and parity (primiparous versus multiparous).
We will assess discrimination, calibration, and other relevant metrics to identify any differential performance.

We will report subgroup results transparently and present any meaningful performance gaps to the CAB, which will consider model refinement, threshold adjustment, or targeted implementation strategies to avoid reinforcing disparities in access to perinatal mental-health care.

We systematically incorporated feedback from two independent grant-review processes into this protocol, refining study design, outcome definitions, sample size considerations, and stakeholder engagement plans (including the CAB) to enhance scientific rigor and implementation feasibility.

Subjecting the protocol to external scrutiny before model development has enhanced its scientific and operational rigor and aligns the study with bestpractice guidance for transparent, stakeholder-informed prediction model development [88].

text.text: Methodologically, the protocol implements a pre-specified, two-stage analysis pipeline with strict train/test partitioning, procedures to prevent information leakage, and calibration-aware handling of class imbalance, reflecting contemporary best practice for prognostic model development [98].

text.text: We defined explicit go/no-go criteria evaluated on the hold-out sample for external crossvalidation.

The MPT will proceed to prospective validation in new samples only if it meets all criteria: test-set ROC-AUC > 0.70; calibration slope between 0.8 and 1.2 with no severe systematic miscalibration; screening sensitivity > 0.70 at the pre-specified clinical threshold; positive net benefit on decision curve analysis versus treat-all and treat-none across clinically relevant thresholds [100]; and where a biomarker-augmented model is selected, a statistically significant AUC improvement over the self-report model.
text.formatted: The MPT will proceed to prospective validation in new samples only if it meets all criteria: test-set ROC-AUC > 0.70; calibration slope between 0.8 and 1.2 with no severe systematic miscalibration; screening sensitivity > 0.70 at the pre-specified clinical threshold; positive net benefit on decision curve analysis versus treat-all and treat-none across clinically relevant thresholds <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">[100]</ref>; and where a biomarker-augmented model is selected, a statistically significant AUC improvement over the self-report model.

text.text: If any criterion is unmet ("no-go"), we will refine predictors, decision thresholds, or model class and re-evaluate the model internally; external validation will be deferred until criteria are met.

The study adopts a pragmatic approach by evaluating a self-report-only model before considering biomarker augmentation, which preserves feasibility for low-resource antenatal settings and limits laboratory requirements to instances when biomarkers demonstrably add value [46].

We view this as the initial model-development and evaluation stage that would serve to justify prospective validation in new samples.

We will leverage our deeply characterized CIHR-funded Pakistani pregnancy-birth cohort (n = 1,861), with assessments at 10-19 and 22-29 weeks' gestation (early pregnancy and late second trimester) spaced roughly 10 weeks apart.

We aim to develop a MPT that will integrate biopsychosocial factors affecting Pakistani pregnant women to enhance treatment selection precision-who should be treated-based on the prediction of depression status and severity later in pregnancy [101, 102] to prioritize the limited mental health resources for those who are most likely to benefit from treatment, thereby eliminating barriers to access and to fast-track recovery [103].
